channel.title: Discovery on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Discovery on Best of AI

item.title: arXiv
item.description:
Authors upload papers, and readers can search, download, and set up alerts. Cornell University operates it. Most papers in physics and math appear there first.

Papers are not peer reviewed by arXiv itself, so quality varies.

bioRxiv and SSRN serve other fields. arXiv suits physicists and mathematicians.

item.title: ATLAS.ti
item.description:
It supports document coding, memos, networks, and co-occurrence tables. AI coding and summary features suggest codes and condense text, and researchers can accept or edit them. It runs on desktop and in a browser.

It is used in academic research, UX research, and market research. Licenses are sold in student, academic, and business tiers.

NVivo and MAXQDA are the main alternatives. ATLAS.ti suits researchers who want flexible coding and visual network tools.

item.title: BioRender
item.description:
Researchers drag icons into a canvas and edit them to build pathways, experimental workflows, and graphical abstracts. Templates speed up common layouts, and teams share a library. Paid plans allow publication use and export options.

Free accounts have limits on exports and icons, so check the license before publishing.

Illustrator and Inkscape give more freedom but take more time. BioRender suits biologists and biochemists.

item.title: CAS SciFinder
item.description:
Users search by structure, reaction, or keyword and see papers, patents, and suppliers. Retrosynthesis tools suggest routes to a target molecule. Results link to the CAS registry.

Access is by subscription, usually through institutions.

Reaxys is the main alternative. SciFinder suits chemists doing literature and synthesis research.

item.title: ChemDraw
item.description:
Users draw structures, predict properties like NMR shifts, and name compounds from drawings. It integrates with Revvity Signals tools and Microsoft Office. A web version supports sharing.

Licenses are paid, and many universities provide them.

MarvinSketch and Ketcher are alternatives. ChemDraw suits synthetic and medicinal chemists.

item.title: Findmypast
item.description:
Users search census, parish, and military records, and view images of the original documents. Family trees are shared and linked to records. Hints suggest matches.

It is a subscription service.

Ancestry and MyHeritage are alternatives. Findmypast suits genealogists with British and Irish ancestry.

item.title: GraphPad Prism
item.description:
Users enter data in tables, choose analyses such as t-tests, ANOVA, survival curves, or nonlinear regression, and get publication-style graphs. It guides non-statisticians with explanations of results. Dose-response and kinetics fitting are common uses.

It is a paid license, often provided through universities. It is less flexible than R or Python for custom work.

R, Python, and JMP are alternatives. Prism suits bench scientists who want a quick path from data to figure.

item.title: MATLAB
item.description:
It has built-in tools for matrices, signal processing, control design, and statistics. Toolboxes add machine learning, computer vision, and domain-specific functions. MATLAB can generate C code for embedded targets, and an AI assistant helps write code in newer releases.

It is standard in aerospace, automotive, and academic engineering. Licenses cost money, though many universities provide them to students, and Octave and Python are free alternatives.

MATLAB suits engineers who need validated toolboxes and a well-documented workflow.

item.title: NASA ADS
item.description:
Researchers search by author, object, or topic, and export references to BibTeX and other formats. It shows citations and metrics, and links to the full text where available. Libraries and observatories also use its API.

It is run by the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory with NASA support. Coverage outside its core fields is thinner.

Semantic Scholar and Google Scholar are broader. NASA ADS suits astronomers and astrophysicists.

item.title: NVivo
item.description:
Researchers import text, audio, video, and PDFs, then tag passages with codes and look for themes. Queries, matrices, and visual maps help compare groups and cases. Newer versions include AI-assisted coding and summaries, which researchers should still check.

Social scientists, health researchers, and market researchers use it for projects with many sources. It is expensive for individuals, though universities often hold site licenses.

ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA are close alternatives. NVivo suits researchers who need an organized system for large qualitative projects.

item.title: Praat
item.description:
Users load recordings, view spectrograms, annotate segments, and run scripts for batch analysis. It also supports speech synthesis experiments. The interface is old-fashioned but very capable.

It is open source and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

ELAN is useful for annotating video and audio. Praat suits linguists studying phonetics.

item.title: Publishers Marketplace
item.description:
Literary agents use it to see which editors buy which kinds of books and to post their own deals. Authors use it to research agents. A daily newsletter lists new book deals.

Data is mostly reported by members, so it is not a complete record.

Query Tracker helps authors track submissions. Publishers Marketplace suits literary agents.

item.title: Sketch Engine
item.description:
Users search for words and phrases, see collocations, and compare usage across corpora. A word sketch summarizes grammatical patterns for a word. Users can also build corpora from their own texts.

It is a subscription service, with free access for some academic users.

AntConc is a free desktop alternative. Sketch Engine suits linguists and terminologists.

item.title: Stellarium
item.description:
Users pick a location and date to see stars, planets, and satellites, and can control telescopes through plug-ins. It includes sky cultures and deep sky catalogs.

A web version runs in the browser, and desktop apps exist for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Cartes du Ciel is another open-source option. Stellarium suits astronomers and amateur observers.

item.title: TinEye
item.description:
It finds copies, edits, and earlier versions, and sorts by date. Fact-checkers use it to trace the origin of a photo. A browser extension and API are available.

Coverage is limited to images it has indexed, so a lack of matches is not proof of originality.

Google Lens and Yandex Images are alternatives. TinEye suits fact-checkers verifying images.

item.title: Wolfram Mathematica
item.description:
Users work in notebooks that combine code, results, and text. The Wolfram Language has built-in functions for a huge range of math and data tasks. It connects with Wolfram Alpha knowledge and, in newer versions, with language model tools.

Licenses are paid, and student editions are cheaper.

MATLAB and SageMath are alternatives. Mathematica suits mathematicians who need symbolic power.

item.title: WorldCat
item.description:
Users search for books, articles, and media, then see which nearby libraries own a copy. Librarians use the underlying records for cataloging and interlibrary loan. OCLC runs the service for member libraries.

Records vary in quality between contributing libraries.

Library of Congress and Google Books are other sources. WorldCat suits librarians and researchers hunting for physical items.

item.title: AlternativeTo
item.description:
AlternativeTo answers a simple question: what else is there like this? You look up an application, such as Photoshop or Slack, and see a list of alternatives, ordered by how many users have liked them, with filters for platform, license, and features. Each entry has a description, screenshots, and user comments, which makes it easy to compare. The site covers software across desktop, mobile, web, and services.

It is useful when you want to avoid a subscription, move to open-source software, find something that runs on Linux, or replace a service that has shut down. Users can propose new applications and vote on alternatives, which keeps the site current. In recent years, it has added extensive coverage of AI tools, with categories for chatbots, image generators, and coding assistants.

item.title: Dia
item.description:
Dia puts an AI assistant at the center of web browsing. The address bar accepts both web addresses and questions, so you can search, ask about the page you are viewing, or have the assistant work across several open tabs, such as comparing products or summarizing a set of articles. It can draft writing in context and pull from what you have open.

The browser keeps familiar elements such as tabs and extensions, but adds features that use browsing history and open pages as context, with options for custom skills that package repeated prompts. It focuses on helping with everyday tasks like research, email drafts, and shopping comparisons.

item.title: Easy With AI
item.description:
Easy With AI is a simple catalog. Visitors browse categories such as writing, image generation, and productivity, read a short description, and follow a link to the tool.

Small directories provide another view of the market, though coverage and updates vary. Details such as pricing change often and should be checked on the product’s site.

The site is free. Similar resources include Futurepedia, There’s An AI For That, Future Tools, Aixploria, and Best of AI. Easy With AI suits people browsing for tools.

item.title: Elasticsearch
item.description: Elasticsearch stores documents as JSON and indexes them so searches come back in milliseconds, even across billions of records. It began as a full-text search engine for things like product catalogs and website search, and it is also used heavily for logs, metrics, and security data. It is the core of the Elastic Stack, which adds Kibana for dashboards, and ingestion tools for getting data in. Companies use it wherever they need to search or aggregate a large volume of text-heavy data quickly.

item.title: FamilySearch
item.description:
FamilySearch lets anyone explore their family history without paying. Users search a vast collection of historical records, including census, birth, marriage, death, immigration, and military records, from many countries, and many are digitized images. A collaborative family tree combines contributions from millions of people, so you can often find relatives and connect with branches others have researched.

Technology plays a large role in making records searchable. Handwriting recognition and machine learning transcribe and index scanned documents at scale, which has opened up collections that would take volunteers years to index by hand. Tools suggest possible record matches for people in your tree, and photo and story features preserve family memories. The service also operates local centers and online help.

item.title: Find an AI Tools
item.description:
Find an AI Tools is a simple list of AI products organized by category. Users browse to see what exists in areas like writing, design, and coding, then click through to the tool.

As with other directories, coverage depends on submissions, and descriptions can lag behind product changes. It is best treated as a starting point.

The site is free. Always check pricing and privacy on the tool’s website. Similar resources include Futurepedia, There’s An AI For That, Easy With AI, Aixploria, and Best of AI. Find an AI Tools suits people scanning for AI tools.

item.title: FutureHouse
item.description:
FutureHouse works on automating scientific research. The lab builds language-model agents that read and reason over the research literature, and makes some available to scientists on a platform. Crow answers questions with cited sources from papers, Falcon performs deeper literature reviews, and Owl helps check whether a topic has been studied.

A more ambitious project, Robin, links agents into a multi-step workflow. Agents suggest hypotheses, plan experiments, and analyze results, and the lab used the system to propose a candidate treatment, which was then tested experimentally. The goal is to speed up discovery by letting agents handle parts of the loop.

item.title: Maltego
item.description:
Maltego is known for visual link analysis. An investigator starts with an entity such as a domain name, email address, or company, then runs transforms that pull related data from sources like DNS records, social media, breach databases, and corporate registries. The results appear as a graph that shows how things connect, which makes patterns easier to see than in a list.

The tool is widely used in cybersecurity and open-source intelligence work. Threat analysts trace infrastructure behind attacks, fraud teams look for networks of related accounts, and journalists and researchers map ownership and connections. A marketplace of data integrations extends what the graph can query, and collaboration features let teams share findings.

item.title: Meilisearch
item.description:
Meilisearch focuses on delivering relevant results quickly with little configuration. Developers send their documents to it through a simple API, and it returns ranked results as the user types, with typo tolerance, synonyms, filtering, and sorting working out of the box. That makes it popular for adding search to a store or a knowledge base.

Newer features address AI. Hybrid search combines keyword matching with vector similarity, so a query can find results by meaning as well as exact words, and it can connect to embedding models. Teams can host Meilisearch themselves, since it is open source, or use the company’s managed cloud.

item.title: Mendeley
item.description:
Mendeley helps researchers organize the papers they read. Users import PDFs, and the software extracts details such as the title and authors, stores them in a library, and lets them highlight and annotate. A Word plugin inserts citations and builds a reference list in thousands of styles, which saves hours when writing papers and theses.

It has social and discovery elements, including groups for sharing libraries and a catalog of research papers. Syncing across the desktop, web, and mobile keeps a library available wherever you work. Elsevier acquired the company, which led some researchers to prefer open alternatives because of concerns about data and lock-in.

item.title: OpenTools
item.description:
OpenTools is a catalog for finding AI products. Visitors search or filter by what they want to do, see short descriptions and pricing information, and follow links to the tools. Beyond products, the site lists models and Model Context Protocol servers, which are useful to developers building agents.

Guides and news help readers understand what is new and how to use tools well. Builders can submit their products for listing, which is how most directories grow.

item.title: Product Hunt
item.description:
Product Hunt started as a simple list of cool new products and became a standard place for startups to debut. Makers submit a product with a tagline, description, images, and a link, and the community upvotes and comments throughout the day. Top-ranked products earn visibility, and a launch can bring early users, feedback, and press attention. The site covers apps, developer tools, hardware, and books.

For readers, it’s a way to see what is new. You can browse by day, week, or month, follow topics such as artificial intelligence, productivity, or design, and read discussions that often include makers answering questions. Collections and newsletters curate products, and a leaderboard highlights trending launches. Makers can also post updates and use the site’s tools to share a launch checklist and gather reviews.

item.title: Scopus
item.description:
Scopus indexes scholarly journals, books, and conference papers across science, technology, medicine, social sciences, and the arts and humanities, and tracks citations among them. Researchers use it to search literature, follow citation trails, and find related work. It’s curated: content must meet quality criteria to be included, which gives the database a reputation for reliability.

Institutions rely on Scopus for research evaluation. It provides author profiles with h-index and other metrics, journal rankings such as CiteScore, and tools for analyzing the output of departments and universities. Funders and universities use these numbers in assessments, rankings, and hiring, which makes the database influential, and sometimes controversial because of the weight put on metrics.

item.title: SemiLaunch
item.description:
SemiLaunch gives small makers a place to announce a product. Makers submit their project, which appears in a weekly cohort, and visitors browse, vote, and comment. Top products are highlighted, helping early-stage founders gain attention and feedback.

The weekly format differs from daily launch sites, giving products more time to collect votes. Listings also serve as backlinks and discovery for new tools in directories.

Visibility depends on community size. SemiLaunch has a free tier and paid promotion options. Alternatives include Product Hunt, Peerlist, BetaList, Indie Hackers, and Dang.ai. SemiLaunch suits indie makers looking for launch exposure.

item.title: Typesense
item.description:
Typesense is built for instant search experiences, like the results that appear as a user types in a store or documentation site. It keeps its index in memory for speed, handles typos by default, and supports filtering, faceting, sorting, and grouping. Its API is simple, and client libraries exist for popular languages.

It also supports modern retrieval needs. Vector search lets applications find results by meaning using embeddings, and hybrid search combines that with keyword matching. Built-in features can generate embeddings, and a conversational search mode answers questions using retrieved documents. Developers can run Typesense on their own servers or use Typesense Cloud.

item.title: Waze
item.description:
Waze built its reputation on live information from drivers. Users report traffic jams, accidents, speed traps, road hazards, and closed roads as they happen, and others see the alerts immediately. The app uses that crowd-sourced data, together with anonymous speed information from devices, to route around slowdowns and update arrival times, often finding shortcuts that other apps miss.

The app is free and has features suited to everyday driving. It shows fuel prices, offers voice navigation with customizable voices, lets you plan drives to leave at a set time, and supports carpool matching in some areas. It integrates with Android Auto and Apple CarPlay and connects to music and calendar apps. Local communities of volunteer editors help keep maps accurate.

item.title: Web of Science
item.description:
Web of Science is one of the oldest and most influential indexes of scholarly literature. It covers curated sets of journals, conference proceedings, and books and records which works cite which, making it possible to follow ideas forward and backward through the literature. Researchers use it to find relevant papers, track citations, and analyze trends in a field.

Institutions also use its data for research evaluation. Clarivate publishes the Journal Citation Reports, which includes the impact factor, one of the most discussed metrics in academia, and Web of Science supports measures of authors, journals, and institutions. A Research Assistant adds AI-driven features such as natural language search and summaries of results. The selectivity of coverage is a selling point and also a criticism, as it favors certain journals and languages.

item.title: AI Directory
item.description:
AI Directory is one of many catalogs that try to keep up with the flood of AI products. Visitors can browse tools by category or search for a use case, such as writing, image generation, coding, or video, and see short descriptions with links to each tool’s own site.

Directories help with discovery. New tools appear constantly, and a list organized by task is easier to scan than a search engine. Makers can submit their products for listing, which is how most such sites grow, so coverage depends on who submits and how closely entries are reviewed.

item.title: Ancestry
item.description:
Ancestry is a genealogy service. Users build a family tree and the site suggests matching records, such as birth certificates, census pages, immigration lists, and military files, from its collection. Hints appear as you add relatives, which helps trace lines back through generations.

Technology helps both records and relatives. Handwriting recognition and machine learning transcribe old documents so they become searchable, and the DNA test connects users with genetic relatives and estimates ethnic origins. Members can share trees and message distant cousins, which often breaks through research dead ends.

item.title: Hunchly
item.description:
Hunchly is a browser extension for investigations. As a researcher browses, it saves each page as it appeared, with screenshots, timestamps, and hash values that help show the content has not been altered. Pages are organized into cases, so evidence from a long investigation stays together.

The tool adds notes, tags, and a way to search across captured content. Reports can be generated for sharing or for legal use. It is popular with open-source intelligence investigators, journalists, and fraud and law enforcement analysts who need to preserve content that may disappear.

item.title: MyHeritage
item.description:
MyHeritage is a genealogy service. Users create a tree, and the site suggests matches in historical records and in other members’ trees, helping them find ancestors and living relatives. A DNA test adds ethnicity estimates and connects users with genetic relatives.

The company is known for photo tools. It can colorize black-and-white pictures, enhance old photos, and animate faces in family photographs, which went viral and made genealogy more emotional for many users. Other AI features transcribe and search documents.

item.title: Rayyan
item.description:
Rayyan streamlines a laborious step in evidence synthesis. Researchers import search results from databases, and multiple reviewers screen titles and abstracts, marking papers as included or excluded, often blind to each other’s decisions. The tool tracks conflicts and helps resolve them.

Machine learning ranks the unscreened papers by likelihood of relevance, so the likely includes surface earlier and screening can end sooner. Highlighting of keywords and filtering by terms speeds reading. Newer features use AI to assist with extraction and summaries.

item.title: Reaxys
item.description:
Reaxys is a chemistry research database from Elsevier. A chemist can search by structure, reaction, or property and find experimental data on compounds, along with the reactions used to make them and the sources. This helps plan syntheses and avoid repeating known work.

Predictive synthesis tools propose routes to a target molecule by combining literature data with machine learning, ranking options by feasibility. It also covers properties, bioactivity, and patent chemistry, serving drug discovery and materials work.

item.title: Algolia AI Search
item.description:
Algolia is a hosted search service known for speed. Developers send it their data, such as products, articles, or help center pages, and use its APIs and UI libraries to add search that responds as the user types, with typo tolerance, filters, and facets. Many e-commerce and media sites use it.

Its AI search layer extends that with newer methods. Hybrid search blends keyword matching with vector similarity so queries find results by meaning, and tools can personalize ranking from user behavior. Merchandisers can adjust relevance with business rules without code, and the platform supports retrieval for conversational and agent experiences, where an AI model answers using the retrieved content.

item.title: Aixploria
item.description:
Aixploria collects AI tools in one searchable catalog. Visitors can browse by category such as writing, image generation, coding, video, and productivity, or filter by price type, and see short descriptions with links to the tools. Popularity rankings and lists of new additions help surface what is trending.

The site also publishes news and selections of the best tools for particular tasks. For someone trying to find a product for a specific need, a catalog like this saves time compared with searching the web. As with any directory, it reflects submissions and the editors’ choices, so entries vary in depth.

item.title: AllThingsAI
item.description:
AllThingsAI is a directory with an emphasis on comparison. Visitors can browse tools by category, then open pages that set two or three similar products side by side, covering pricing, features, and user feedback. This helps when you have already narrowed the field and need to decide between close options.

The site covers a wide mix of tools, from writing assistants to image and video generators. Like other directories, it relies on submissions and editorial curation, so details can lag behind fast-moving products. Comparison pages are most useful as a starting point.

item.title: Dang.ai
item.description:
Dang.ai is a place to discover AI tools through community voting. Makers submit their products, users upvote them, and the top entries appear on the homepage. Categories cover writing, image, coding, video, and other areas, with each listing showing a short description and a link.

The model rewards recent launches, so it suits people who want to see what is new and popular. Voting can reflect marketing effort as much as quality, so rankings are a starting point. Comparing listings across several directories gives a better picture.

item.title: Future Tools
item.description:
Future Tools is a directory of AI products maintained by Matt Wolfe, who covers AI on YouTube. Instead of accepting every submission automatically, the site reviews tools before listing them, which keeps the collection more selective than open directories.

Visitors browse by category, such as writing, video, productivity, and coding, or sort by what has been popular, and the site highlights new additions. Each listing has a short description and a link to the tool. A newsletter shares updates.

item.title: Futurepedia
item.description:
Futurepedia is a directory of AI tools with a focus on helping people choose. Visitors browse by category or use case, filter by price, and read short descriptions and reviews. New listings are added regularly, so it can serve as a way to keep up with launches.

The site also publishes tutorials, courses, and a newsletter aimed at people who want to apply AI in their work. Like other directories, it relies on submissions and editorial choices, and some listings may be promoted.

item.title: Insidr.ai
item.description:
Insidr.ai is a directory with an emphasis on learning how to use tools. Instead of listing products only by category, it groups them by what people want to accomplish and publishes guides that show how to combine tools for a task.

That approach helps newcomers who know their goal but not the products. Guides cover topics like content creation, research, and marketing, with step-by-step ideas. The site also tracks new tools as they appear.

item.title: There's An AI For That
item.description:
There’s An AI For That, often shortened to TAAFT, started as a simple search for AI tools by task. A user types what they want to do, such as write a cover letter or remove a background, and gets a list of tools for that job, with ratings and descriptions.

Its size is the draw. It adds new tools constantly, offers an alert for launches, and includes pricing and user reviews. Some listings are promoted by makers.

item.title: Toolify.ai
item.description:
Toolify.ai is a large AI tool directory. Visitors browse categories, search by task, and sort by popularity measures such as estimated monthly traffic and rankings. Each listing has a description, pricing, and links.

Traffic-based ranking offers a different view from editorial picks, showing what people are using. It can favor tools with strong marketing, and estimates are approximate.

The site is free to browse, with paid promotion for makers. Verify claims on the product’s own site. Similar resources include There’s An AI For That, Futurepedia, Aixploria, OpenTools, and Best of AI. Toolify.ai suits people tracking which AI tools are popular.

item.title: TopAI.tools
item.description:
TopAI.tools is a directory where the community votes for tools. Makers submit products, users upvote them, and rankings reflect that interest. The approach aims to give newer and smaller products visibility.

Listings include pricing information, categories, and short descriptions. Filtering by category helps users narrow down choices.

Voting can reward good marketing as much as quality. The site is free. Similar resources include Product Hunt, There’s An AI For That, Futurepedia, Dang.ai, and Best of AI. TopAI.tools suits people exploring newly launched AI tools.

item.title: Best of AI
item.description: Best of AI is a directory for finding AI tools without wading through hype. It lists tools by what they do, across more than a hundred categories such as code assistants, image generation, and meeting assistants, and by who uses them, with profession pages for designers, developers, marketers, lawyers, teachers, and many others. Each tool has a page with a description, category, price tier, website, tags, and links to alternatives.

item.title: Submit AI Tools
item.description:
Submit AI Tools collects AI products in a searchable list. Visitors browse by category, read short descriptions, and click through to the tools. Makers submit listings to get discovered.

As with other directories, coverage depends on submissions and editorial review, so details can be incomplete or out of date. It works best as one of several places to scan.

The site is free. Check each tool’s own site for pricing and privacy information. Similar resources include Futurepedia, There’s An AI For That, Aixploria, OpenTools, and Best of AI. Submit AI Tools suits people browsing for AI products.

item.title: Marketinguys
item.description:
Marketinguys works as a directory of marketing talent. Businesses looking for a freelancer or agency can browse profiles, compare specialties such as SEO, social media, or branding, and reach out to candidates.

Directories like this save time in the first round of research, though quality varies and vetting is the buyer’s job. Check portfolios, references, and contracts before hiring.

Independent information is limited. The platform is free to browse. Alternatives include Clutch, Upwork, Fiverr, DesignRush, and Sortlist. Marketinguys suits businesses looking for marketing help.

item.title: Perplexity Pro
item.description:
Perplexity is an answer engine that searches the web and writes cited responses. The Pro tier raises limits on advanced searches and lets users choose among models, including Perplexity’s own and leading models from other labs, for harder questions.

Pro adds tools for research: upload and analyze documents, longer and more detailed searches, image generation, and access to deeper research modes that produce reports. Spaces let users organize topics and collaborate, and an API credit is sometimes included.

item.title: AI For Developer
item.description:
AI For Developer is a niche directory focused on the developer audience. Instead of listing every AI product, it gathers tools that matter to people who write software: coding assistants, AI-powered editors, model APIs, testing and documentation tools, and infrastructure for building AI features. Listings give a short description, links, and categories, which makes it easy to browse by use case.

Directories like this serve as a starting point for discovery. They help developers learn what exists, compare similar tools, and keep up with the rapid pace of new launches. A curated approach aims to reduce the noise of general AI directories that include thousands of products across every field, by focusing on relevance to engineering.

item.title: AIDir.wiki
item.description:
AIDir.wiki collects information about AI products in a wiki format. Each entry describes a tool or model, notes what it is for, lists key features and pricing information, and links to the official site. Because it is community-maintained, contributors can add new tools and update existing entries as products change, which is meant to keep information fresher than a static list.

The wiki structure encourages cross-linking, so related tools, alternatives, and categories connect. Visitors can browse by category or search for a specific product, and use it as a reference when comparing options. It joins a broad field of AI directories, from curated lists to large databases, and positions itself as an open, collaborative resource.

item.title: Altern
item.description:
Altern is a browsable directory of AI products. Visitors can search by task or browse categories, such as writing, design, coding, and video, and see short descriptions, pricing, links, and user ratings. Rankings and filters aim to surface popular and well-regarded tools so people do not have to sift through thousands of options alone.

Tool makers can submit their products to be listed, and users can leave ratings and reviews. The directory also offers comparisons and alternatives for specific products, which is useful when you already know one tool and want to see similar ones. Like other discovery sites, it covers a wide range from established products to new launches.

item.title: Andi
item.description:
Andi is a search engine for people who find link lists cluttered. You ask a question, and it returns a short answer with cited sources, plus links you can open. The idea is to combine the answering ability of a language model with the freshness of the web.

Privacy and design are part of the pitch. Andi has said it does not rely on advertising or sell user data, and the interface is clean, with options to refine a query and explore related questions. It is one of several startups, along with Perplexity, You.com, and Phind, that took on the conventional search model.

item.title: Apple Maps
item.description: Apple Maps comes installed on every Apple device and has improved a great deal since its rocky start. It provides turn-by-turn driving directions, walking, cycling, and public transit routes, plus lane guidance and speed limit information. Features such as Look Around give a street-level view of many cities, detailed maps show buildings and landmarks in 3D, and downloadable offline maps work without a connection. Guides collect recommended places in a city, and you can share your arrival time with friends.

item.title: Arc Browser
item.description: Arc reimagined the browser. Instead of a row of tabs across the top, it uses a vertical sidebar where tabs are grouped into spaces, such as work and personal, each with its own pinned items and theme. Tabs that you do not use are archived automatically, and features like split view, boosts for customizing websites, and easels for collecting ideas made it a favorite of power users and designers. It is built on Chromium, so most Chrome extensions work.

item.title: Bing Chat
item.description: Bing Chat was Microsoft’s first big move into AI-assisted search. It put a conversational assistant next to the Bing search box, so you could ask a question and get a written answer with links to sources instead of scanning a page of results. Microsoft later renamed and expanded it as Copilot, and the assistant now works across the web, in the Edge browser, in Windows, and in standalone mobile and desktop apps.

item.title: Devv.ai
item.description: Devv.ai was built as a search tool for programmers, positioned between a traditional search engine and a chatbot. You ask a technical question, such as how to configure a library or why an error occurs, and it searches documentation, GitHub repositories, and developer discussions and then writes an answer with sources. Linking to sources helps you verify the answer, which matters because chatbots can invent APIs or settings that do not exist.

item.title: Dimensions
item.description:
Dimensions connects different kinds of research outputs. Instead of searching only for papers, users can see how a grant led to publications, which patents cite a study, and whether a trial or policy document refers to it. The linked structure helps trace the path from funding to impact.

Institutions, funders, and researchers use it for several purposes. Universities benchmark their output, funders track results of the grants they award, and companies look for experts and emerging fields. AI features summarize results, help with literature searches, and surface connections, and APIs let organizations pull data into their own systems.

item.title: Dovetail
item.description:
Dovetail gives research teams a home for customer feedback. Researchers upload interviews and other data, and the platform transcribes recordings, lets them highlight key quotes, and organizes everything so insights can be found later. Teams build a searchable repository instead of losing findings in slide decks.

AI shortens the analysis step. It tags content automatically, groups related feedback into themes, summarizes sessions, and answers questions across a body of research. Reports and shareable highlights help researchers communicate with product teams and executives, and integrations pull in data from support and survey tools.

item.title: Elicit
item.description:
Elicit helps researchers move through academic literature faster. A user asks a research question, and Elicit searches a large database of papers, presents relevant results, and extracts details such as sample size, methods, and outcomes into a table. Seeing structured comparisons across studies is much quicker than reading each paper in full.

Additional tools support systematic review work. Users can screen papers against criteria, summarize findings, and build reports, with citations tied to the passages in each paper so claims can be checked. It is used by students, academics, and professionals in evidence-based fields.

item.title: Exa AI
item.description: Exa, formerly Metaphor, rethinks search for machines instead of people. Where a traditional engine matches keywords, Exa uses neural embeddings to find pages that are semantically similar to a query, even when they do not share words. You can search with natural-language descriptions, such as a list of startups building a specific kind of robot, and it returns results that match the idea. It can also take a link and find similar pages.

item.title: Explainpaper
item.description: Explainpaper targets a familiar frustration: academic papers are dense and full of jargon. You upload a PDF, select the sentence, equation, or paragraph you do not understand, and the tool gives a plain-language explanation. You can adjust the level, from a lay audience to an expert, and ask follow-up questions about the paper. It was popular with students and curious readers who wanted to follow a paper outside their own field.

item.title: Foursquare
item.description:
Foursquare began as an app for checking in at places and discovering venues, but its main business today is location data. The company maintains a large database of points of interest, including businesses, landmarks, and venues, with details like categories, hours, and popularity. Developers use its Places API to add search, recommendations, and place information to maps and apps, and brands use its data to understand where people go.

Beyond place data, Foursquare provides tools for analyzing movement and location behavior. Panels of opted-in users allow measurement of foot traffic to stores, audience analysis, and attribution for advertising, and mapping and geospatial products let companies visualize and process location data at scale. Machine learning keeps place information up to date and helps match records from different sources.

item.title: Google Maps
item.description: Google Maps is the default map for much of the world. It provides turn-by-turn navigation with live traffic and rerouting, public transit schedules, walking and cycling directions, and detailed maps with business hours, photos, reviews, and popular times. Street View lets you look at places at ground level, Live View uses your phone’s camera to show directions as arrows in the real world, and offline maps work without a connection.

item.title: Inciteful
item.description:
Inciteful takes a paper or a list of papers and builds a network of the research that surrounds them. Using citation data, it identifies the papers that are most connected, which tend to be foundational works, review articles, and recent developments. You enter a DOI, title, or several seed papers, and the tool shows a ranked list of papers, authors, and journals, with visual graphs of how they connect.

It is most useful early in a literature review. Starting from a few papers you know, you can discover similar and influential work you might have missed, track the most cited authors in the area, and spot new papers that cite your seeds. A Paper Discovery view finds the most important papers connected to your starting point, and a Literature Connector finds papers that link two different topics. Results can be exported to reference managers.

item.title: Kagi
item.description:
Kagi takes a different business model from other search engines: users pay a subscription, and in return there are no ads, no tracking-based profiles, and no incentive to favor advertisers. Results are meant to be clean and relevant, and the company says it does not sell data. The service uses several sources, including its own index of smaller sites, and puts effort into reducing low-quality content and SEO spam.

Control is a defining feature. Users can raise, lower, or block domains, so a site that is always useless for you disappears, and lenses restrict a search to a set of sources, such as forums or academic sites. AI tools include summaries of pages and videos, answers with citations, and an assistant that gives access to multiple language models. Kagi has also launched Orion, a privacy-focused browser, and other products around the search experience.

item.title: Lens.org
item.description:
The Lens aims to make innovation data open. It combines a very large database of patents from patent offices worldwide with scholarly works from sources like Crossref, PubMed, and others. Users can search by keywords, inventors, institutions, or classifications, and the results show patent families, legal status, citations, and links to the full text where available. The free access sets it apart from commercial patent databases.

The key feature is the connection between patents and papers. It tracks which scholarly works are cited in patents, which lets researchers and technology transfer offices see how academic research is used in inventions, and lets innovators find prior art. Collections let you save and share sets of results, and analytics and dashboards visualize trends, such as top applicants or fast-growing technology areas. Sequence search supports biotechnology patents.

item.title: NotebookLM Plus
item.description: NotebookLM Plus gives heavier users more room in NotebookLM, Google’s tool for working with your own documents. The free version lets you add sources, ask questions with citations, and generate study aids, but it limits the number of notebooks, sources, and daily queries. The Plus tier lifts those limits, so people with large projects, such as researchers, students writing theses, or analysts working across many documents, can keep more material in one place.

item.title: OpenRead
item.description:
OpenRead is built for people who read a lot of research. After you import a paper, an AI assistant can answer questions about it, explain terms, summarize sections, and pull out items like methods, results, and limitations. A structured summary view lays out the main points in a consistent format, which helps when scanning many papers for a review.

The platform extends beyond a single paper. It helps search the literature, organize papers into collections, take notes alongside the text, and generate outlines or review drafts from selected sources. Support for multiple languages makes it useful for researchers who read in a second language, and translation features help with papers published in other languages.

item.title: Paper Digest
item.description:
Paper Digest helps researchers keep up with a flood of new papers. Instead of scanning listings of new submissions every day, a user sets up topics or keywords and gets a personalized digest with short AI-generated summaries of matching papers. This helps researchers spot relevant work quickly and decide which papers merit a full read.

The service also publishes curated summaries of papers from major conferences and journals, and offers a platform to search, summarize, and organize papers. Paper Digest builds on text summarization models to produce abstracts and key points, and it provides tools such as a reader and a way to generate a quick literature overview. Some features are open to everyone, while others sit behind a login or subscription.

item.title: Perplexity
item.description: For research, Perplexity is useful because it shows its sources. Each answer comes with numbered citations to the pages it used, so you can open the link and check a claim before relying on it. You can narrow searches to particular kinds of sources, such as academic papers, and keep asking follow-up questions that build on the earlier ones. This makes it a quicker starting point than a list of search results for questions that need several sources.

item.title: Perplexity AI
item.description:
Perplexity positions itself as an alternative to the list of links. You ask a question in natural language, it searches the web in real time, reads the pages, and writes a concise answer with citations to each source. That format is helpful for questions where you want a quick overview with a way to check the evidence, such as product comparisons, news, how-to questions, and research basics.

The experience supports continued exploration. Follow-up questions build on earlier context, and focus options narrow the search to categories such as academic sources or discussion forums. Pro Search runs more steps for complex questions, and Deep Research generates longer reports. The Comet browser brings the assistant into everyday browsing, and Spaces organize related research. Users can choose among several models in paid plans.

item.title: Perplexity Labs
item.description: Labs goes beyond answering a question. You describe a project, such as a market analysis, a financial model, or a small dashboard, and Labs works for several minutes, combining web research, code execution, and chart creation. It then returns finished assets: a written report, a spreadsheet, charts, or a simple web app that you can download or share. The tool uses a team of specialized steps behind the scenes, so the output is more like a deliverable than a chat reply.

item.title: Perplexity Pages
item.description:
Pages is a publishing layer on top of Perplexity’s research. After you explore a topic with the assistant, you can convert the thread into a structured page with headings, summaries, and citations to the sources it used. It organizes the material in the way a short article or study guide would be written, instead of leaving you with a conversation log.

You control the result. Sections can be rewritten, reordered, or removed, images can be added, and the page can be published with a shareable link or kept private. Educators use Pages to create study guides, students for report drafts, and professionals for quick explainers on topics they research often. Because the citations travel with the content, readers can check where claims came from.

item.title: Phind
item.description: Phind was built for programmers who had questions that a standard search engine handled poorly. A developer could ask how to fix an error, compare libraries, or write a function, and Phind searched the web and documentation, then wrote an answer with code snippets and links to its sources. It used its own coding-focused models and later offered an IDE extension and a chat interface for follow-up questions, and it was popular as a free alternative to general chatbots.

item.title: Productivity Directory
item.description:
Productivity Directory collects tools that help people work better. Instead of listing every AI product, it focuses on productivity: task managers, calendars, note apps, automation, meeting assistants, and writing aids. Each listing has a short description, a category, and a link, so visitors can browse by need and compare similar tools quickly.

Directories like this serve people early in their search. A user who wants to improve how they plan their day or take meeting notes can see what exists and narrow down options before visiting individual sites. Editors choose which products to include, which gives it a more focused feel than massive catalogs, and new tools are added over time.

item.title: Scinapse
item.description:
Scinapse is a search tool for scientific literature. It indexes a large body of scholarly papers across disciplines and ranks results with machine learning that considers relevance, citations, and recency. Users search by topic, title, or author, filter by year, journal, and field, and read abstracts with links to the publishers or open-access copies.

Features go beyond a basic list. Author pages show a researcher’s publications and citation profile, paper pages show who cited a work and related papers, and collections let you save papers to read later. Alerts notify you about new papers on a topic or from an author. The site was created by a Korean research technology company and is free to use, supported by its broader services for researchers.

item.title: SciSpace
item.description: SciSpace, formerly known as Typeset, is built around the problem of reading dense research. Upload a PDF or open a paper from its database, and an AI copilot lets you highlight a passage, a table, or an equation and ask for an explanation in simpler terms. You can also ask questions about the whole paper, request a summary, or get the key methods and results. It is helpful for students and researchers entering an unfamiliar field.

item.title: Semantic Scholar
item.description: Semantic Scholar is a research search engine built by the Allen Institute for AI, a nonprofit research organization. It covers hundreds of millions of academic papers across science, medicine, engineering, and the social sciences, and it is free. Unlike a plain keyword search, it uses language models to understand what papers are about and how they connect, which helps surface relevant work that does not use the exact words you typed.

item.title: Undermind
item.description: Undermind is designed for the situation where a simple search leaves you wondering what you missed. You describe your research question in plain language, including constraints and nuance, and the agent runs a deep search: it queries multiple sources, reads abstracts and text, follows citations, and refines its search based on what it finds. After some minutes, it delivers a ranked list of relevant papers with explanations of why each matches.

item.title: Wolfram Alpha AI
item.description: Wolfram Alpha doesn’t search the web. It computes answers. Ask it to integrate a function, convert units, compare populations, or show the weather on a given date, and it uses curated data and algorithms, written in the Wolfram Language, to produce a result with steps, charts, and data. That makes it reliable for math, physics, chemistry, statistics, and factual queries with definite answers, which is where language models often make mistakes.

item.title: Yelp
item.description:
Yelp built its business on reviews. Users write about their experiences with restaurants, home services, medical offices, and other local businesses, rate them, and upload photos. Search results combine ratings, distance, price, and filters such as open now or takeout, which helps people choose. In the United States, it is a major source for restaurant and service recommendations.

Businesses can claim their listing, add information, respond to reviews, and run ads, and some features support booking, waitlists, and requesting quotes from local professionals. AI has been added to the product: assistants help users find places through conversation, summaries condense long review histories, and tools detect and filter spam and fake reviews through a recommendation software that sorts reviews by reliability.

item.title: You.com
item.description:
You.com is a search engine that mixes web results with AI-generated answers. You ask a question and receive a conversational response with links to sources, along with traditional results and apps for tasks like coding or image creation. A privacy focus has been part of its positioning, with a private mode and a commitment to not selling personal data.

The product has moved toward agents and enterprise search. Research and agent modes run multi-step investigations and produce longer reports, a custom agent builder lets people create assistants for specific tasks, and the platform lets users switch among models from different providers. For developers and businesses, You.com offers APIs that deliver live web search results formatted for AI applications, which several AI companies use to ground their answers.

item.title: Zotero
item.description:
Zotero saves references with a click. A browser connector captures a paper or web page along with its citation details and PDF, and the library organizes items in collections with tags and notes. Word and Google Docs plugins insert citations in thousands of styles.

Group libraries support collaboration, and the open ecosystem has plugins for annotation, syncing, and AI summaries and search. Because it is community driven and non-profit, users keep control over data.

item.title: Connected Papers
item.description: Connected Papers helps you get oriented in a research area. You enter a paper title, DOI, or link, and it produces a graph where each node is a paper and closer nodes are more similar. Similarity comes from co-citation and bibliographic coupling, meaning papers that cite similar sources or are cited together, rather than from keywords. Node size and color show citation count and year, which lets you see influential and recent work at a glance.

item.title: Iris.ai
item.description: Iris.ai aims to reduce the time scientists spend finding and reading relevant papers. Instead of keyword searches, a researcher can input a problem description or an abstract, and the system finds related papers by meaning. It then helps explore the results with a visual map of topics, filters based on content, and tools that extract data and summarize findings across many documents. Research teams use it to scan a field, check for prior work, and decide where to focus.

item.title: Scite
item.description: Scite changes how citation counts are read. A paper with many citations may be well supported or heavily disputed, and a raw count does not tell you which. Scite analyzes the text around each citation and labels it as supporting, contrasting, or mentioning, with a snippet of the citing sentence, so you can see how others have actually used a finding. It helps researchers judge reliability and spot controversial claims.
